title: General Claude usage, documentation and addons
author: Middle_Ad630
selftext:
Hello, 

I’ve been working on a game for some time now and it’s getting bigger and bigger.   
Sometimes I feels that Claude loses track of already set rules and plan even though we use docs for everything and I also try to keep up and document the steps.  
With all that, the other issue is the token usage that’s getting heavier.

I’d love to know if you guys have some tips or experience when it comes to larger scale game dev with AI.  
What strategies you use. How often you start new chats with the agent.  
If you are using Claude cowork or code   
Or if you have experience with Claude addons to improve workflow and token usage. (I’m so skeptical here reading how many say that you have to use things like PonyTail and so on while others say that it can drastically reduce the quality of the work of Claude)

Maybe some of you can share some of their own experience with me! :)

comments.author: Bavariasnaps
comments.body:
>Sometimes I feels that Claude loses track of already set rules and plan even though we use docs for everything 

where exactly are the rules located? Important rules should be in an [agents.md](http://agents.md) or an [architecture.md](http://architecture.md) you link from the [agents.md](http://agents.md) to

comments.author: Left-Prompt7557
comments.body:
In terms of starting new chats, I try to do /clear between discrete tasks as it can help with token usage.

I generally use Claude code+vscode+unity. I've been used to vscode since pre-AI and like that I still have the control to edit code if I need to - but I'll be totally honest, I rarely need to these days.

In terms of keeping context, if it's not doing it already, ensure your agent is updating it's ledger with key decisions and rules. There is a token cost to doing this in more detail, but it will help address forgetting rules.

comments.author: Harvan29
comments.body:
Solo dev on a fairly big Unity game (trading/strategy), built with Claude Code. I hit both of your problems in October, and they turned out to be one problem: too much stuff loaded into every session.

What fixed it:

* **Measure first.** I checked what a fresh session loaded before I typed anything: \~70k tokens. About 20k of that was tool names from MCP connectors I wasn’t using, \~10k was skill descriptions, and the rest was my own memory and doc files, some close to 200 KB. You pay for all of it again on every turn.
* **Short rules file, long docs somewhere else.** My root [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) only holds what applies to *every* session: language, git rules, code conventions, “ask before spending credits”. The design doc is a separate file that gets opened only when it’s needed. Rules in a short file get followed. Rules on page 30 of a design doc don’t.
* **Memory as state cards, not a diary.** One index file, one line per topic. Each topic is a card under 8 KB: what it is, where it stands, my decisions, known traps, which files. At the end of a session the card gets *updated*, not appended to. Old history goes into an archive folder that never loads unless I ask for it. A new session reads the index plus the 1–3 cards for what we’re working on.
* **Every rule gets a “why”.** A rule with a reason is followed much better than a bare “don’t do X”.
* **Engine gotchas in a skill.** All the Unity traps (play mode, compiling, saving scenes) are in one project skill that loads only when the session touches Unity.
* **Read less.** Big files (scenes, logs, long docs) get grep or head, never read whole.
* **One session per task**, not one endless chat. The cards carry the context from one session to the next.
* **One agent, one step at a time.** No multi-agent teams. When I do run parallel sessions, each one gets written boundaries: which files and scenes it owns.

I use Claude Code, not Cowork. I haven’t tried PonyTail. My approach is the opposite: every skill or connector you install adds its description to every session, so I keep few of them and turn connectors on only in the session that needs them.

replies.author: Capybarhigh
replies.body:
Your message and this thread made me ask how my project was going, and I got some cool stuff out of it. The most important thing was that command that he asked me to run. It exposed the issues I had in my project and we discuss them to fix them.

    /doctor prompt-audit

I'm leaving this comment here hoping it can help someone else!

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
You need a documentation! It saves you more then you spent for it. I usually never start a new chat but use one to deligate all jobs. One chat keeps the context running unless I'm starting sth different. Every deligated agent has only the context it needs. 
Opus 5.5 as main, codex as coder and Gemini as researcher and in code search agent.

comments.author: ttyttyq
comments.body: Turn rules into hooks that way they can't be ignored

comments.author: Mental_Tailor_4227
comments.body: You can also add a Canary effect, to make sure Claude remembers everything from your document. Works well and you know when it’s not following said document

comments.author: david-song
comments.body:
I've done multiple 100k LoC projects with Claude and Codex, and the things that bite are very similar to a software project written by humans.

If you don't have everything designed up front then you'll need to develop with future changes in mind. Agents tend to do the minimal thing required to make a feature that you ask for, they'll do it using the words you use to describe them, and they'll add special cases to get a job done right now without considering what it costs in future. If you don't set boundaries and fold things back into higher level concepts you'll be left with "tight coupling" where code is complex (braided) by being tangled up with things it has no business knowing about, and have "low cohesion", where parts that change together are scattered through the codebase.

A patronising example that doesn't work like this in reality (at least with Opus 5.5 or Fable), but it's the sort of pattern to look out for. Say you have pigs in your game, and they oink occasionally. Then later you add in that they squeal when they're attacked. Later on you add dogs, these bark when alerted and they whimper when hit. Chances are, if you didn't look at or ask about the structure of the code you'll get two parallel systems, one that deals with barks and one that deals with oinks, one that deals with hits and one that deals with attacks; a bunch of special cases with hard-coded values. What you really wanted was an animal system with health and some kind of AI state with alertness, fear, hunger and so on, with call and cry events that have a side effect of a sample playing. You want a system where dogs and pigs are mostly the same thing but with different specialisations. But do pigs have alertness? Do they "hunt" for truffles maybe? You need to own these decisions and provide a bit of guidance here, and if you don't then you might end up with dog\_hunger being a different thing to pig\_hunger. Then later when you change how one of them works then it'll only change that one, they'll need to be read and edited in multiple places, the logic will diverge so they're different things, then the differences are relied on later so merging them together is impossible or breaks things that end up balanced on top.

This sort of thing applies everywhere, to your game's timer, weather systems, path finding and collision, player inventory, to the materials things are made of. It applies to your UI and NPC AI and the general structure of your game.

The solution is to stop parallel systems from forming, to complain about divergence, demand that things are simplified and combined where possible, to be refactored as you add features. Discuss strategies for making things generic, make the agent justify special cases that add complexity, push back against them. Don't accept the quick fixes. Do clean-up passes after adding features, and bluntly ask awkward questions about whether this is becoming shit code - you should be aiming for elegance and simplicity rather than a tangled web of references and fractals of nested branching logic.

Refactoring is expensive work, it's best to minimize the need for it with a decent enough design up front. But honestly, weeding the garden as you go is the best solution we've ever had, and the amount of code that AI generates makes it more important than ever.

edit:

Also I see people talking about documentation and having the agents write more stuff down. I have extremely mixed results with this, it can quickly grow into an expensive mess. In this agentic age the docs are a form of code, and you need to refactor those too. Thin down slop bombs and dev diaries as they emerge, or they'll eat into your context with every edit.

comments.author: Any-Blacksmith-2054
comments.body: Definitely context overflow; compact everything to some md's and start new chat. I'm doing it quite often, for every new feature or when context >70%
